questions.explain: Azure SQL Managed Instance offers near-100% compatibility with on-premises SQL Server — including SQL Server Agent, CDC, and cross-database queries — inside your own VNet, making it the natural lift-and-shift target.
options: Azure SQL Database serverless single database, which drops Agent and CDC
Azure SQL Managed Instance, with near-100% on-premises compatibility including Agent and CDC
Google Cloud SQL for SQL Server, which leads in SQL Server feature depth
A self-managed EC2 instance, which is the only option supporting CDC
questions.q: Which managed SQL Server offering does the chapter call the natural lift-and-shift target from on-premises?

questions.explain: RDS Multi-AZ maintains a synchronous standby in a different AZ that is not addressable for reads — it exists purely for failover, typically completing in 60-120 seconds with a 5-second DNS TTL.
options: Yes — it serves read traffic automatically via read-only routing
Yes — but only queries marked ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly
Yes — Multi-AZ DB clusters expose all standbys for reads
No — the standby exists purely for failover and is not addressable for reads
questions.q: Can applications run read queries against an RDS Multi-AZ standby?

questions.explain: RDS automated backups combine daily snapshots with transaction log backups every 5 minutes, enabling point-in-time recovery to any second within the 1-35 day retention window. A restore creates a new instance — factor instance-launch and log-replay time into RTO.
options: RDS combines daily snapshots with transaction log backups every 5 minutes for point-in-time recovery; a restore creates a new instance
RDS takes hourly full backups only, with no transaction log backups and no PITR
RDS restores in place over the existing instance in under 60 seconds
RDS automated backups are sufficient, so manual snapshots are never needed
questions.q: Which statement about RDS automated backups and point-in-time recovery is correct per the chapter?

questions.explain: The chapter's encrypted-connections query selects encrypt_option and auth_scheme from sys.dm_exec_connections — the direct way to verify TLS enforcement (rds.force_ssl on RDS, TLS enforced by default on Azure SQL Database).
options: sys.dm_exec_sessions, which stores the certificate thumbprint per session
sys.configurations, which lists the negotiated cipher suite
sys.dm_exec_connections via the encrypt_option column
sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states, which tracks TLS per AG replica
questions.q: How do you verify that client connections to a cloud SQL Server are actually encrypted?

questions.explain: The db.r family is memory-optimized, and SQL Server's buffer pool benefits disproportionately from RAM — so for SQL Server on RDS the db.r family is almost always the right choice.
options: db.t4g, because burstable instances are safe for production under sustained load
db.r, because the buffer pool benefits disproportionately from RAM
db.m7g only, because memory-optimized instances waste money on databases
The smallest instance class, because cloud storage I/O replaces buffer pool memory
questions.q: For SQL Server on RDS, which instance family does the chapter recommend, and why?
